phonemes.desc: Open vowel [a] followed by alveolar nasal [n], the first element of a Sumerian/Akkadian theophoric compound.
Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ] followed by long [aː] and tapped [r]; the name means 'whole sky' or 'totality of heaven'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ahn-SHAR' — the š is like the sh in 'ship', and the second syllable is drawn out with stress.

pronunciation.note: The name is written in cuneiform as 𒀭𒀭𒊹. The ASCII form anshar flattens the distinctive š consonant to plain sh digraph; the restoration Anšar recovers the standard Assyriological transliteration. Because it preserves the postalveolar fricative š, the entry is placed in Tier 1.

domains.title: The Whole Sky
domains.subtitle: Primordial Heaven and Cosmic Totality
domains.lead: Anšar is the primordial sky of Babylonian cosmogony, the 'Whole Heaven' that arises from the mingling of the primordial waters Apsû and Tiāmat. With his consort Kišar, the Whole Earth, he forms the second generation of gods, the parents of Anu, and the ancestors of the great divine assembly. He is less a personal god than a cosmic principle: the upper half of the created order, the vast dome that contains the stars, the winds, and the gods themselves.

cards.name: Primordial Sky
cards.desc: The upper half of the cosmos, born from the mingling of fresh and salt waters.

cards.name: Father of Anu
cards.desc: With Kišar he begets Anu, the sky god, beginning the dynasty of the great gods.

cards.name: Cosmic Boundary
cards.desc: Heaven as the limit and container of the visible world, paired with earth below.

cards.name: Ancestor of Marduk
cards.desc: Through Anu and Ea, Anšar is the great-grandfather of Marduk, king of the gods.

symbols.name: The celestial dome
symbols.meaning: The bowl of heaven, the visible sky as the body of Anšar.

symbols.name: Circle or ring
symbols.meaning: The šar element suggests totality, circumference, and the full circle of the sky.

symbols.name: Upper waters
symbols.meaning: Heaven as the region above the waters, separated from the earth below.

symbols.name: Starry field
symbols.meaning: The fixed stars and planets set in the dome of Anšar.

mythology.lead: Anšar's mythology is concentrated in the Babylonian creation epic Enūma Eliš. He is one of the primordial gods who arise from the first waters, the father of Anu, and the ancestor from whom Marduk will eventually spring. His role is cosmogonic rather than narrative: he names the structure of the world before the world has heroes.

myths.title: Birth from the Waters
myths.text: In the beginning, according to Enūma Eliš, there was no heaven and no earth, only Apsû the sweet waters and Tiāmat the salt waters. Their mingling produced Lahmu and Lahamu, the silt deposits at the edge of the waters, and these in turn produced Anšar and Kišar, the Whole Sky and the Whole Earth. The pair thus represents the first cosmic differentiation into upper and lower.

myths.title: Father of Anu
myths.text: Anšar and Kišar together beget Anu, the great sky god of later Mesopotamian religion. Anu in turn begets Ea (Enki), and Ea begets Marduk. Anšar therefore stands at the head of the divine genealogy that culminates in Marduk's kingship over the gods.

myths.title: The Council of the Gods
myths.text: When Tiāmat raises an army of monsters to avenge Apsû's death, the younger gods are terrified. Anšar, as the eldest of the assembled gods, summons the divine council and eventually appoints Marduk as champion to face Tiāmat. His authority is that of the senior ancestor, the voice of cosmic order against chaos.

myths.title: Sky as Totality
myths.text: The name Anšar is sometimes parsed as 'whole sky' or 'totality of heaven'. It is not merely the sky as a region but the sky as the complete upper half of the cosmos, the counterpart and complement of Kišar's earth. The pair expresses the binary structure — above and below, male and female, bounded and bounding — that underlies much ancient Near Eastern cosmology.

etymology.derivation: The name is Akkadian: an 'heaven' + šar 'totality, whole'. It forms a pair with Kišar (ki 'earth' + šar 'totality'). The etymology is clear and is supported by the parallel structure of the two names and by their role in Enūma Eliš as the primordial sky and earth.

originalScriptNote: The name is written in Sumero-Akkadian cuneiform as 𒀭𒀭𒊹 — the divine determinative followed by signs read An-šar. The Unicode restoration Anšar is a scholarly transliteration; the cuneiform form is not registrable in the .com IDN table. Because the restoration preserves the postalveolar fricative š, the entry is Tier 1.
syncretism: Anšar has no extensive independent cult or foreign syncretisms. His importance is entirely cosmogonic: he is the primordial sky from whom the later sky god Anu descends. In some scholarly interpretations, Anšar represents an old Akkadian personification of the horizon or the upper firmament, absorbed into the Enūma Eliš genealogy. The Greek Ouranos and the Egyptian Nut share the role of celestial parent, though no direct historical connection is attested. Anšar's primary significance remains his pairing with Kišar as the first cosmic differentiation.
culturalLegacy: Anšar's legacy is literary and cosmological rather than cultic. The Enūma Eliš, in which he appears, was recited at the Babylonian New Year festival and shaped Mesopotamian ideas of cosmic order for more than a millennium. The pairing of Anšar and Kišar as heaven and earth is one of the earliest expressions of the binary cosmology found across Eurasia. In modern scholarship, Anšar serves as a key figure in discussions of Mesopotamian creation theology and the development of the Marduk cult. His name occasionally appears in fantasy and occult contexts as an archaic sky power.
extendedMeditation:
Anšar invites us to think about boundaries. Before there were cities, kings, or temples, there was the great division: above and below, sky and earth, order and chaos. Anšar is the upper half of that division, the container in which everything else will happen.

To meditate on Anšar is to meditate on the horizon. He is not the storm or the star but the dome that holds them. In a world that often feels fragmented, his name reminds us that the ancient cosmos was imagined as a single, bounded whole — a marriage of heaven and earth from which all particular things descend.

archaeology: Anšar has no independent temples or cult images. His presence in the archaeological record is entirely textual, above all in copies of Enūma Eliš from Assyrian and Babylonian libraries such as Ashurbanipal's collection at Nineveh. The epic was copied and recited for more than a thousand years, ensuring the name's preservation in the cuneiform corpus.
